title: Scale It Yourself: a Traffic Simulator Lab
oneLiner: Add load balancers, caches, replicas, a CDN, queues and a rate limiter to a web service under rising load and failures, and watch latency, errors, saturation and cost.
keyTakeaway: Scaling is finding the saturated tier and fixing that one. Stateless app servers scale out behind a load balancer; caches and CDNs remove work instead of adding machines for it; read replicas scale reads but not writes; queues move slow work off the request path but still need enough workers; rate limiters stop abuse before it costs anything; and timeouts with circuit breakers keep one slow dependency from tying up every server. Plan capacity for the bad day: a lost server, a cold cache, a spike.
explanation:
This lab puts the building blocks from the rest of the section together. You run a small online shop: users load static files (images, scripts), read product pages through an API and place orders. Each scenario sends traffic for two simulated minutes, sometimes with a failure partway through, and gives you a goal: a p99 latency, an error rate, sometimes a monthly budget. Add and configure components until the run passes, then read why the fix worked. The Sandbox lets you set traffic and failures yourself.

How to read it. The chart shows traffic, p50 and p99 latency and the error rate for every second. The tier cards show how busy each part is at the second you pick with the time slider: utilization is offered work divided by capacity. Watch the card that turns red first. That tier is the bottleneck, and adding capacity anywhere else changes nothing, which is the most common mistake in real capacity planning and in interviews.

Why latency explodes near 100%. A tier that is 50% busy makes a request wait about twice its own service time; at 90% about ten times; at 98% fifty times. That is the shape of a queue: when work arrives at random, the closer you run to full, the longer the line. So healthy systems run at 50% to 70% at peak, and the cost readout shows what that headroom costs. Past 100%, a tier can't keep up at all: the excess is rejected or times out.

The model, stated plainly, because it is a teaching model and not a benchmark. Each app server has 4 CPU cores (4,000 ms of CPU per second) and can hold 100 requests open at once. A static file costs 2 ms of app CPU, a product page 6 ms plus 3 database queries (or one cache lookup), an order 8 ms plus 2 queries plus 60 ms of side work (resizing images, sending emails) unless a queue takes it. Half of product pages call a recommendations service that normally answers in 40 ms. A database node handles 3,000 queries a second; writes go to the primary and reads to the replicas if there are any. The CDN serves 95% of static files from the edge. A worker runs side jobs at 4,000 ms of CPU a second. Network time is about 60 ms to your datacenter and 15 ms to a CDN location. Every tier's average time is its service time divided by (1 - utilization); a request's time in each tier is drawn from an exponential distribution with that average, 200 sample requests per second from a seeded generator, so the same settings always give the same result. Requests over 3 seconds count as errors, as do requests a saturated tier turns away. Prices are round made-up numbers for comparing designs, not real cloud prices.

Things the model leaves out, which matter in real systems: autoscaling delays (new servers take minutes to start), replication lag and stale reads from replicas, cache invalidation, a database's write limit (only sharding raises it), network bandwidth, and retries, which can turn overload into a retry storm (see Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers and Load Shedding). Use it to build intuition about bottlenecks and headroom, then check real numbers with load tests against your own system.
